extracted.intended_audience: Employers covered by OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, chemical manufacturers/importers/distributors, safety and health professionals, and stakeholders/commenters in the rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: HCS economic analysis and compliance criteria
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts OSHA's analytic assumptions, unit-cost rules, and compliance accommodations used to estimate costs and savings from updates to the Hazard Communication Standard (labels, SDSs, training, and small-container rules). Useful for employers and commenters assessing compliance burden and economic impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management familiarization time estimates (establishments affected by revisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimates management familiarization time for establishments that will incur additional costs because of the rule (i.e., affected establishments) as 1 hour for small establishments, 4 hours for medium establishments, and 16 hours for large establishments of a Health and Safety Specialist's labor time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These final FEA estimates double the PEA's preliminary times based on commenter evidence about update complexity. Multiplying these hours by the loaded hourly wage of $61.18 yields per-establishment costs of $61.18 (small), $244.73 (medium), and $978.92 (large). These per-establishment values are then multiplied by counts of affected establishments to derive aggregate costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management familiarization time estimates (indirectly affected establishments)
rubrics_metrics.description: For establishments that will not incur costs beyond rule familiarization ('indirectly affected establishments'), OSHA estimates management familiarization time of 0.25 hours for small establishments, 1 hour for medium establishments, and 4 hours for large establishments of a Health and Safety Specialist's labor time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplying these labor burdens by the loaded hourly wage of $61.18 results in per-establishment costs of $15.30 (small), $61.18 (medium), and $244.73 (large). OSHA left these preliminary per-establishment labor burdens unchanged where commenters provided no supporting evidence to rebut them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment size definitions (for cost categorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA defines establishment size categories used in the analysis as: small establishments = fewer than 20 employees; medium establishments = 20 to 499 employees; large establishments = 500 or more employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These size bins are used to assign different unit-time and cost burdens and to multiply by counts of establishments (e.g., OSHA estimated 38,018 small establishments with additional costs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training cost inclusion criterion (which workers require incremental training)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA includes incremental training costs only for health and safety personnel who are already trained under the 2012 standard but need additional training to become familiar with updates to SDSs and labels for impacted aerosols, desensitized explosives, and flammable gases. OSHA does not include retraining costs for downstream users or general worker populations when hazards have not substantively changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: hazards remain the same (only classification changes), so downstream users typically need only trivial notification; including retraining would double-count baseline training costs. Stakeholder claims to the contrary must provide quantitative details to change this assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training unit time and unit cost assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit assumptions used for training cost calculations: 2.5 hours of a Health and Safety Specialist's time to prepare training materials; production workers spend 12 minutes receiving the training. OSHA used loaded hourly wages of $61.18 (Health & Safety Specialist), $60.37 (logistics personnel), and $31.09 (production workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inputs yield unit costs of $152.96 (prep by specialist), $12.07 (logistics personnel training), and $6.22 (production worker training). OSHA multiplied these units by the counts of affected firms and workers to produce total undiscounted one-time training costs ($0.96 million) and annualized costs ($136,953) using the agency's discounting method (see annualization rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of retraining for downstream users (double-counting avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA declines to add costs for retraining all workers because such time would double-count (1) baseline training already assigned costs in the 2012 FEA and (2) the incremental training estimated in this FEA; downstream users' hazards have not changed and thus usually require only trivial additional training/notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments asserting broader retraining costs must provide quantitative evidence of increased required training time per worker; absent such evidence OSHA retains its preliminary incremental training assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary method for going from per-establishment/unit costs to national annualized estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA calculates aggregate costs by multiplying per-establishment (or per-worker) unit costs by numbers of impacted establishments/entities or workers to produce an undiscounted one-time cost, then annualizes that one-time cost using a 7 percent discount rate over a 10-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: management familiarization undiscounted one-time cost of $8.0 million annualized at 7% over 10 years yields $1.1 million in annualized costs. This method is applied consistently across cost categories (training, SDS updates, management familiarization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Released-for-shipment compliance option and label-updating rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the finalized paragraph (f)(11), chemical manufacturers/importers/distributors may opt not to relabel chemicals that have been released for shipment; if they choose not to relabel, they must provide an updated label for each individual container with each shipment. OSHA removed the proposal to require a 'released for shipment' date on labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA treats this change as an optional compliance mechanism: firms will choose the cheaper approach (relabel before shipment or supply updated labels with shipments). OSHA reasons the creation of an updated label is not a new cost compared to the 2012 HCS baseline; commenters concerned about feasibility or cost can choose to relabel instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-savings estimation methodology for released-for-shipment provision
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's cost-savings estimate for the released-for-shipment option is based on: (A) an assumed average relabeling cost equal to 50 percent of product value (derived from CPDA survey range 1.5%–204% and capped practically at ~100%); (B) the percentage of products warehoused for more than six months (assumed 5%); (C) the percentage of warehoused products relabeled in any year due to new hazard information (assumed 1%); and (D) the percentage of products in each NAICS industry covered by the HCS (assumed 100% for manufacturing; specific estimated fractions for wholesale NAICS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA multiplied these factors by average product values and counts of affected firms (using ERG and Economic Census data where needed) to estimate annual cost savings (summed across six affected industries) of $33.3 million. OSHA invited comments on these parameters and retained them where no substantive rebuttal data were provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small and very-small container labeling accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(12) permits abbreviated labeling for 'small containers' (volume capacity ≤100 ml) requiring only: product identifier, pictogram(s), signal word, chemical manufacturer's name and phone number, and a statement that full label information is on the immediate outer package. For 'very small containers' (volume capacity ≤3 ml), if any label would interfere with normal use, only the product identifier is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These accommodations codify prior letters of interpretation for small containers and introduce new guidance for very small containers. OSHA estimated no incremental cost savings for small containers (because industry already uses practical accommodations) but estimated potential savings for very small containers where labels interfere with use.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDSs / electronic template update cost driver
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's estimated costs for revising SDSs and labels are directly related to the number of SDSs (i.e., the number of electronic templates) affected by revisions to Appendices C and D; affected SDS/template counts were previously derived in Tables VI-5, VI-6, and VI-7 and used to compute Table VI-14 cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated costs by NAICS and establishment size for modifying electronic templates are incorporated into the aggregate costs presented in Table VI-12. The agency treats SDS/template counts as the primary driver of label/SDS update costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of contractor/vendor pricing for SDS/label updates
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's analytic position is that vendor prices for producing an SDS or label will be folded into companies' normal update cycles; therefore, the full cost of hiring a contractor to produce an SDS or label should not be attributed entirely to the HCS updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites this principle in response to commenters (e.g., NACD) who argued vendor prices would raise agency cost estimates. OSHA requests commenters to provide data on how contractors' costs would be differentiated or the magnitude of underestimates to alter this assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contractor/third-party data and Economic Census to allocate affected product shares by NAICS
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct data were unavailable, OSHA used contractor (ERG) analyses and 2012/2017 Economic Census data to estimate the percentage of product lines in NAICS industries that are covered by the HCS (e.g., estimated 41.7% of NAICS 424910 were fertilizers in earlier ERG work, updated to 37.1% in 2017 data; NAICS 424950 estimated at 77.6% then updated to 82.0%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses these NAICS-based fractions to scale industry-level average product value and number-of-entities inputs when estimating industry-specific costs and cost savings for provisions like the released-for-shipment exemption and small-container accommodations. Commenters were invited to provide alternative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and comment evidence standard for revising analytic assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's practice in this FEA is to retain preliminary assumptions where commenters provide no quantitative data or specific evidence to rebut agency estimates (e.g., hours, unit costs, percentage assumptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ameren and NAIMA provided qualitative or aggregate claims about higher training or labeling costs but did not supply per-worker time estimates or other quantitative details that would enable OSHA to change its assumptions, so OSHA left its preliminary estimates unchanged.
